title: Three ways to think
goal: Give and ask for opinions with the right "think" verb, and talk about plans and predictions with *tänker*, *planerar*, *ska* and *kommer att*.
bekal: you can choose between *tycka* (opinion), *tro* (belief) and *tänka* (thinking, intending)
you can talk about plans with *ska*, *tänker* and *planerar att*
you can make predictions with *kommer att*
wave: Go back to Unit 1: tell what you did last weekend in five sentences, then add your opinion to each one with *Jag tyckte att…* (*Jag tyckte att filmen var tråkig*).

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Vad tycker du?
dialogs.intro: A Sunday evening in the kitchen of the shared flat on Södermalm. Jonas has just played Dian a recording of his band's new song, and the talk soon turns to the summer.

lines.text: Dian, vad tycker du om vår nya låt? Vi spelade in den igår.
lines.id: Dian, what do you think of our new song? We recorded it yesterday.
lines.literal: Dian, what think you about our new song? we played in it yesterday.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag tycker att den är jättebra! Men refrängen är lite för lång, tycker jag.
lines.id: I think it's really good! But the chorus is a bit too long, if you ask me.
lines.literal: I think that it is giant-good! but chorus-the is little too long, think I.

notes: **Vad tycker du om vår nya låt?** — here *om* is a plain preposition ("about, of") and is **not** stressed: *vad TÜK-ker dü om*. Compare the particle verb from Unit 3, *tycka om* (to like), where the stress jumps to the particle: *jag tycker **OM** låten* = I like the song. Same words, different stress, different meaning.

**…tycker jag** — Swedes love to tack *tycker jag* or *tror jag* onto the end of a sentence to soften it, a bit like English "…if you ask me" or "…I think". Note the inverted order (*tycker jag*, not *jag tycker*): the whole sentence before it counts as the first element, so the verb comes second.

**Jag tror inte att jag hinner** — just like English "I don't think I'll make it", Swedish usually negates the *tro*, not the clause after it. *Jag tror att jag inte hinner* is grammatical but sounds heavier. *Tro* (**troo**) is for facts you're not sure about: *Jag tror att tåget går kl. 8*.

**Jag tänkte på en sak** — *tänka på* (**TENG-kah poh**) = to think about, to have something on your mind. Swedish has no progressive form, so the simple past *tänkte* covers English "I was thinking" as well.

**Vad tänker ni göra i sommar?** — followed directly by a base form, *tänka* means "to intend, to plan to": *Jag tänker åka till Dalarna* = I'm going to go to Dalarna (I've made up my mind). No *att* here! *Planera*, on the other hand, does take *att*: *Vart planerar ni **att** åka?*

**Klart vi kommer!** (**klaht**, the *rt* drops its *r*) — short for *Det är klart att…*, "of course". **Förresten** (**fö-RES-ten**) = by the way. And **midsommarstången** (**MID-som-mahr-stong-en**) is the leafy, flower-covered pole Swedes dance around at midsummer — more on that in Unit 20.

grammars.title: Tycka, tro, tänka
body: English "think" does three different jobs. Swedish gives each job its own verb — and choosing the wrong one is one of the most common learner mistakes.

head: Verb
Used for
Quick test
Example
rows: a belief about facts; a guess
Can it be checked — is it true or false?
Is your brain busy with it — or have you decided?

after: Compare: *Jag tycker att det är kallt* (to me it feels cold — my opinion) and *Jag tror att det är kallt* (I suppose it's cold outside — I haven't checked).
In questions and short answers, the pattern is the same: *Tycker du det?* (Is that your opinion?) — *Tror du det?* (Do you really believe that?)

grammars.title: The future: ska or kommer att?
body: Swedish has no single future tense. Instead you choose by asking: is someone **deciding** this, or am I just **predicting** it?

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: a plan still being worked out

after: One special case: *Det ska regna imorgon* means "it's supposed to rain tomorrow" — you are passing on what the forecast says. *Det kommer att regna* is your own prediction.
In speech *att* often disappears: *Det kommer bli dyrt*. In writing, keep it.

blocks.text: Swedish conversation values consensus. Rather than a flat *Du har fel* (you're wrong), most Swedes go for *Jag håller inte riktigt med* or *Jag tycker nog lite annorlunda*. Strong opinions are fine — but they're usually wrapped in a small cushion.

blocks.title: Short answers with det
items: Swedes answer opinions with a fronted *det*: *Det tycker jag också.* (I think so too.)
To disagree, put *inte jag* at the end: *Det tycker inte jag.* (Not me.)
Same pattern with *tro*: *Det tror jag.* (I think so.) — *Det tror jag inte.* (I don't think so.)

head: Svenska
Pronunciation
English
rows: to be thinking of, to consider

blocks.text: **Jag funderar på att…** is the gentlest way to share a plan that isn't settled yet: *Jag funderar på att flytta till Göteborg* = I'm thinking of moving to Gothenburg. Note that Swedes plan far ahead — friends book a *fika* two weeks in advance, and summer cottages are rented in January. "Let's see on the day" is not a very Swedish approach.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 2
items: Combine plans with the time clauses from Unit 2: *När jag har tagit examen tänker jag söka jobb.*
*Innan vi åker på turné ska vi spela in tre låtar.*
Make two sentences of your own with *när*, *innan* or *efter att* + *ska* or *tänker*.
